AE582 · SATELLITE ENGINEERING

Attitude Determination & Control

Mission requirements → pointing → disturbances → determination → control → sizing → verification

This lecture treats ADCS as a mission-design problem: what must the spacecraft point at, how accurately, what tries to rotate it, and what hardware closes the requirement with margin?

Earth-observation running caseLive disturbance budgetSensor tradeWheel sizingControl response
1 · MISSION DRIVER

ADCS exists because the mission needs a direction

Three things that must point

  • Payload: camera boresight to the target.
  • Antenna: link axis to the ground station.
  • Solar array / thermal surfaces: favorable orientation to Sun and space.
Images: [1].

Higher pointing performance can mean better imagery, higher data rate, or more generated power.

Running case: EO CubeSat

Mission inputBaseline
Orbit altitude550 km
Science pointing0.10°
Jitter target0.02° over exposure
Off-nadir slew30° in 60 s
Control concept3-axis active
1 · MISSION DRIVER

Attitude is orientation, not position

Six degrees of freedom

Translationx · y · zRotationroll · pitch · yaw

ADCS focuses on rotational motion about the spacecraft center of mass. Orbit determination/control is related but distinct.

Systems coupling

  • Orbit sets atmospheric density and magnetic field.
  • Attitude changes drag area and solar-array incidence.
  • Mass properties set rotational response.
  • Payload, telecom, power and thermal impose pointing constraints.
1 · MISSION DRIVER

The ADCS design loop is iterative

The FireSAT design sequence [4] and the NanoSTAR preliminary design [3] use essentially this logic. This lecture walks the same loop with one spacecraft.
What must point?Payload, antenna, arrays, radiators: each sets a direction and an accuracy.
What disturbs it?Drag, gravity gradient, solar pressure and magnetic torques, set by orbit and geometry.
What closes it?The lightest sensor and actuator set that meets every mode with margin.
2 · REQUIREMENTS

Accuracy, knowledge, control error and jitter are not the same thing

Pointing vocabulary

  • Accuracy / APE: long-term misalignment from the desired direction.
  • Knowledge error: difference between true attitude and the onboard estimate.
  • Control error: difference between commanded and controlled attitude.
  • Stability / RPE / jitter: high-frequency motion around the mean.
Definitions after [2].

Why the distinction matters

A camera can point at the correct scene yet blur it because of jitter. Or it can produce a sharp image of the wrong scene because APE is too large.

Earth observationWhat ground error follows from angular error?Accuracy and jitter both matter.

Pointing requirements tighten from communications through Earth science to astronomy [1].

3 · ATTITUDE DESCRIPTION

Reference frames answer “relative to what?”

Common frames

  • Inertial: fixed with respect to distant stars.
  • Orbital/LVLH: tied to local vertical and velocity.
  • Body: fixed to spacecraft structure.

Earth observation example

Nadir pointing means the camera boresight is constrained relative to the local vertical frame, while a star tracker measures attitude relative to an inertial reference.

The estimator connects these frames.

3 · ATTITUDE DESCRIPTION

Euler angles are intuitive—but the rotation order matters

+Z
—

Human-readable attitude command.

Why order matters

  • Rotate 90° about x, then 90° about z: the result differs from z first, then x.
  • There are 12 valid axis sequences (3-1-3, 3-2-1, …), so a set of angles means nothing without its sequence [1].
  • At pitch = ±90° two of the three axes line up and one degree of freedom is lost: the singularity.
3 · ATTITUDE DESCRIPTION

DCM and quaternion describe the same orientation differently

Direction cosine matrix

Maps vector components between frames. Excellent for analysis and vector transformations.

—

Quaternion

Four parameters, no Euler-angle singularity, convenient for onboard propagation and control.

—

Euler angles are best for interpretation; quaternions are best for robust digital implementation [2].

RepresentationParametersAdvantagesDisadvantagesTypical use
Direction cosine matrix9 (6 redundant)No singularity; no trigonometry; simple product ruleSix redundant parametersAnalysis; transforming vectors between frames
Euler angles3No redundancy; clear physical meaningSingularity; trigonometric functions; awkward for successive rotationsHuman input and output; analytical studies
Quaternion4 (1 redundant)No singularity; no trigonometry; simple product ruleNo obvious physical meaningOn-board propagation and control laws
Comparison after [1] and [2].
4 · DYNAMICS

Angular momentum is the rotational currency

Rigid body

\[\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}\]

Inertia plays the role that mass plays in translation.

External torque

\[\frac{d\mathbf H}{dt}=\mathbf T\]

External torque changes total angular momentum. Internal actuators redistribute momentum between the spacecraft body and wheels.

4 · DYNAMICS

For quick preliminary design, one axis often starts with T ≈ Iα

Angular acceleration—
After 10 s from rest—
show calculation
\[T=I\alpha\]
With the defaults, 2 mN·m on 0.08 kg·m² gives 1.43°/s² and 14.3°/s after 10 s. A disturbance a thousand times smaller still adds up over an orbit.
4 · DYNAMICS

Mass properties are an ADCS input—not a mechanical afterthought

Need from Structures

  • Center of mass and uncertainty.
  • Principal moments of inertia.
  • Products of inertia / alignment.
  • Changes after deployment or propellant use.

Why it matters

  • Slew torque scales with inertia.
  • Gravity-gradient torque depends on inertia differences.
  • CM–CP offsets create aerodynamic and solar-pressure torque.
  • Flexible appendages can couple into the control loop.

Interactive mission model: spacecraft and orbit inputs

5 · DISTURBANCES

Aerodynamic torque can dominate low LEO

\[T_a=\frac12\rho C_D A V^2\,r_{CP}\]
current substitution

What this means for design

  • Above about 200 km the flow is free-molecular, so \(C_D \approx 2\) to 2.2 [1].
  • Density is uncertain by a large factor: size for the high-solar-activity case.
  • The torque arm is the offset between centre of pressure and centre of mass. Moving either one is often cheaper than a larger actuator.
  • Worked example [1]: S = 5 m², h = 400 km, rCP = 0.01 m gives T ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ N·m.
5 · DISTURBANCES

Gravity-gradient torque couples orbit and mass properties

\[T_g=\frac{3\mu}{r^3}|I_{max}-I_{min}|\sin(2\theta)\]
current substitution

Reading the equation

  • The torque scales with the difference of inertias: a sphere feels none.
  • It is largest at 45° from the local vertical and zero when a principal axis points at nadir.
  • It falls with 1/r³, so it matters most in LEO.
  • Worked example [1]: 700 km, ΔI = 30 kg·m², θ = 1° gives T ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ N·m.
5 · DISTURBANCES

Solar-pressure and magnetic torques complete the first-order budget

\[T_{sp}=\frac{\Phi}{c}A(1+q)r_{CP}\]
\[T_m\approx D_m\frac{\lambda M_E}{r^3}\]
DisturbanceDependence on distance from EarthAlso depends on
Aerodynamic≈ e−ar (falls fastest)Solar activity, day or night
Gravity gradient1 / r³Inertia difference, attitude
Solar radiation pressureIndependentEclipse, surface reflectivity
Magnetic1 / r³Residual dipole, orbit inclination
After [1]. In GEO and beyond, solar pressure is usually the largest disturbance.

6 · ARCHITECTURE

Passive or active control?

ConceptPointingTypical accuracy [2]ManeuverabilityMission fit
Gravity gradientCoarse Earth-local1–3°Very limitedSimple Earth-oriented mission
Spin stabilizationInertial spin axis0.1°Slow repointingSimple/scanning missions
MagneticCoarse1°SlowLEO small spacecraft
3-axis reaction wheelsFine0.01°HighEO, astronomy, agile missions
Our 0.1° EO requirement plus repeated off-nadir slews strongly favors active 3-axis control.
Passive stabilization uses a disturbance torque to hold the spacecraft stable; it cannot command a new attitude [1].
6 · ARCHITECTURE

Sensors determine attitude; actuators change it

The real system also contains sensor noise, alignment errors, flexible dynamics, actuator limits and digital delay.

7 · SENSORS

Attitude determination combines references with dynamics

Absolute reference

Star/Sun/Earth/magnetic measurements prevent long-term drift.

Propagation

Gyros provide fast angular-rate information between absolute updates. Filtering combines both, because exact attitude determination is never error-free.
Gyros carry the estimate between absolute fixes; each fix removes the accumulated drift.

What the estimator does

  • Fuses sensors with a model of the spacecraft to estimate attitude and rate.
  • Typical algorithms: extended Kalman filter, unscented Kalman filter [1].
  • Also estimates gyro bias, which is why a modest gyro can support fine pointing.
  • Exact attitude determination is not possible: there is always some error [2].
8 · ACTUATORS

Reaction wheels exchange momentum internally

Torque

\[T_{body}=-T_{wheel}\]

Fast, continuous and precise. Three axes need at least three independent wheel axes; four wheels are common for redundancy.

But momentum accumulates

A secular external torque forces wheel speed to keep changing. Eventually the wheel reaches its speed/momentum limit and must be desaturated using an external torque.

Practical notes [1]

  • Wheels are not run near 0 rpm: friction is nonlinear and zero crossings wear the bearing.
  • One wheel per control axis; a fourth, skewed wheel gives redundancy.
  • Typical small-satellite wheel [2]: 0.02–0.3 N·m torque, 1.3–4 N·m·s storage.

8 · ACTUATORS

Magnetorquers provide the external torque for LEO momentum dumping

\[\mathbf T=\mathbf m\times\mathbf B\]
Magnetic torque is perpendicular to the local field, so instantaneous 3-axis authority is constrained. Orbit variation is part of the design.

Thrusters and CMGs occupy different parts of the design space

ActuatorExternal?Typical pointing [1]StrengthPenalty / use
MagnetorquerYes1–5°No moving parts, no propellantLEO only; field-constrained torque
Reaction wheelNo0.005°Precise continuous controlSaturation; vibration; power
ThrusterYes0.05°Fast, high authorityPropellant, impulse quantization, translation coupling
CMGNo0.005°Very high torqueLarge/complex; used on large agile vehicles
Internal or external?
External actuators change the total angular momentum and are necessary. Internal ones only move momentum around inside the spacecraft [1].

9 · CONTROL

Real control loops include estimation and flexible dynamics

Estimator

Sensor noise, bias, alignment and intermittent references mean the controller never receives “true attitude” directly.

Structure interaction

Solar arrays, booms and flexible payload structures add modes and phase lag. Tight pointing can become a controls–structures problem rather than a rigid-body problem.

Rule from Explorer 1

With any energy dissipation, a spin is stable only about the axis of maximum inertia. A spinner must be a wheel, not a pencil [1], [2].

When the loop goes wrong: the Hitomi failure chain [1]

ADCS closure dashboard: does the EO mission close?

Change any earlier blue input. This dashboard uses the same shared model—requirements, orbit, mass properties, sensors and hardware are not independent decisions.
10 · INTEGRATED DESIGN

Student trade: make the mission close without overdesigning it

Try these perturbations

  1. Lower the orbit to 350 km.
  2. Double the CM–CP drag offset.
  3. Demand a 30° slew in 20 s.
  4. Remove the star tracker.
  5. Reduce wheel momentum storage.

Allowed design responses

  • Change control mode or operational constraint.
  • Move CM / CP or change geometry.
  • Change wheel or magnetorquer sizing.
  • Add/change sensors.
  • Relax a requirement only if the mission permits it.

The goal is not “make every number huge.” It is to close the mission with credible margin.

The mission-design loop closes with evidence

A good preliminary ADCS design can explain why each sensor and actuator exists, what requirement sizes it, and what evidence will verify it.

From mission to requirements

  • Distinguish accuracy, knowledge and jitter.
  • Define ADCS modes from mission operations.
  • Choose useful attitude representations.

From environment to hardware

  • Estimate major disturbance torques.
  • Size reaction-wheel torque and momentum.
  • Understand momentum dumping.
  • Select a sensor suite consistent with the pointing requirement.

2 · REQUIREMENTS

APE and RPE fail the image in different ways

For an EO mission, accuracy and stability are separate requirements. Improving attitude knowledge alone cannot remove wheel-induced jitter.
4 · DYNAMICS

Mass properties are configuration-dependent

What ADCS needs from structures

  • Center of mass in the ADCS reference frame.
  • Full inertia tensor, not only total mass.
  • Products of inertia / principal axes.
  • Uncertainty and evolution after deployments or fuel use.
\[\mathbf H=\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega\]

Mission-design consequence

Deploying a solar array can change inertia, move the center of pressure, alter disturbance torque and change slew performance at the same time.

configuration→I, CM, CP→disturbances→actuator sizing

6 · ARCHITECTURE

Detumbling: use Earth's magnetic field before precision pointing

B-dot concept

A magnetometer measures the changing field in the rotating body frame. The commanded dipole opposes that change:

\[\mathbf m_c=-k_B\dot{\mathbf B}\]

The resulting torque is \(\mathbf T=\mathbf m_c\times\mathbf B\).

Useful because magnetorquers need no propellant and can operate immediately after deployment in LEO.

Rate after 60 min—
Mode exit threshold0.5°/s
7 · DETERMINATION

Sun sensors are excellent acquisition sensors, but not a complete estimator

Coarse/fine Sun sensor
Measures one or two Sun angles. Clear FOV required.

Coverage matters
Multiple heads can provide wide angular coverage, but eclipse removes the reference entirely.

A LEO eclipse must be tolerated without violating pointing constraints [4]. This is why rate gyros and other absolute references are combined with Sun sensors.
7 · DETERMINATION

Interactive: why gyros need an absolute reference

Between updates, bias integrates into attitude error. A star tracker, Sun sensor, horizon sensor or magnetic reference periodically bounds the drift.
7 · DETERMINATION

Attitude determination needs independent geometric information

One vector

A Sun vector or magnetic-field vector constrains the spacecraft to a cone of possible attitudes. Rotation about that measured vector remains unresolved.

Two non-collinear vectors

Two measured body-frame vectors with their known reference-frame directions define a complete triad and therefore a three-axis attitude estimate.

\[\hat i=\frac{u}{|u|},\quad \hat j=\frac{u\times v}{|u\times v|},\quad \hat k=\hat i\times\hat j\]

This is the geometric idea behind TRIAD and related methods; redundant measurements can be combined statistically.

On the celestial sphere each measurement is a cone of possible attitudes with an error band. Two cones cross at two points: the true solution and a false one, which an a-priori estimate or a third measurement rejects [2].
8 · ACTUATORS

Reaction wheels solve one problem and create two new ones

Internal torque
Wheel acceleration produces equal and opposite spacecraft torque.

Microvibration
Static/dynamic imbalance creates speed-dependent disturbances that can drive jitter.

Saturation and vibration are the two penalties of reaction wheels [2]. Torque capability and momentum storage are sized separately [4].

Required torque—
8 · ACTUATORS

Momentum dumping belongs in the operations concept

Why schedule it?

  • Reaction wheels absorb secular external momentum.
  • Magnetorquers or thrusters must return that momentum to the environment.
  • Magnetic unloading can disturb precision pointing and magnetometers.
  • Dump windows may therefore be excluded from science observations.

Mode interaction

Science→wheel H ↑→Dump→recover

This is the ADCS analogue of battery SOC in EPS: a stored quantity accumulates and must be actively managed.

8 · ACTUATORS

Thrusters provide external torque—but placement matters

Force couple

\[T=2FL\]

Matched thrusters can generate a pure torque. Mismatch, timing error or CM uncertainty produces unwanted translation and residual torque.

Mission trade

  • Fast and high authority.
  • Consumes propellant and limits lifetime.
  • Minimum impulse bit can create limit cycles.
  • Plume, contamination and structural loads can matter.

A dead zone with hysteresis prevents chatter and excessive fuel use [2].

On/off thrusters cannot hold zero error. Without a dead zone they “chatter” and waste propellant. With a dead zone and hysteresis the spacecraft coasts between two rate-limited bounds: a slow limit cycle with low fuel use [2].

11 · VERIFICATION

Verification should trace every requirement to measurable evidence

Knowledge

  • Sensor calibration and alignment.
  • Star-field / Sun / magnetic stimulus.
  • Estimator Monte Carlo with bias and noise.

Control

  • Wheel torque and momentum tests.
  • Air-bearing or HIL closed-loop tests.
  • Slew, settling and momentum-dump demonstrations.
Recommended test levels are benchtop and component testing, environmental testing, air-bearing tests and hybrid simulations [2]. The preliminary model tells us what must be measured; verification provides the evidence that the real system matches it.
